cases.title: How far away is hydrogen? Its role in the medium and long-term decarbonisation of the European energy system
cases.source_trace: Saved historical abstract; publisher record also verified. Online 2015, journal issue January 2016.
cases.source_specific_proposition: JRC-EU-TIMES scenario modelling suggested hydrogen could become viable in the EU energy system around 2030 under a long-term carbon constraint; hydrogen might help decarbonise industry and transport.
cases.scenario_condition: Long-term carbon cap; scenario is conditional, not a guarantee or the later EU production target.
cases.radar2_question: Has hydrogen become more practically viable as a European decarbonisation option, and what deployment and cost constraints remain on the path to 2030?

findings.document: European Court of Auditors, Special report 11/2024
findings.evidence: The EU was unlikely to meet the 2030 renewable-hydrogen targets established years after the original paper; market rules, project maturity and demand hinder deployment.

findings.document: ACER, European hydrogen markets monitoring report 2025 (covering 2024 deployments)
findings.evidence: EU electrolyser capacity was 308 MW in 2024, 51% more than before but well behind the 2024 EU policy ambition of 6 GW. Renewable hydrogen production costs were about four times conventional hydrogen costs.

findings.document: JRC, Water Electrolysis and Hydrogen in the EU: 2025 Status Report (published 14 Jan 2026)
findings.evidence: EU operational electrolysis capacity was projected at 514–800 MW by end-2025; high capital costs and raw material dependencies remain.

findings.document: State of the clean Hydrogen Valleys sector 2026
findings.evidence: Publication metadata/abstract: more than 600 MW of electrolyser capacity was operational in Europe, 225 MW above 2024; projects exceeding 800 MW reached final investment decision during 2025 and 3.3 GW was past FID. Its expectation that half of 3.3 GW would operate in 2026 is explicitly a plan, not operational output. LIMITATION: “Europe” may include non-EU jurisdictions and project scopes differ from ACER’s EU measurement. Neither installed electrolysis MW nor FID directly verifies the 2015 EU system-model threshold for viability or hydrogen use in industry and transport.

findings.document: Global Hydrogen Review 2026: executive summary
findings.evidence: Global hydrogen demand exceeded 100 million tonnes in 2025, nearly all used in existing industrial/refining applications; low-emissions production grew 20% to almost 1 million tonnes, still under 1% globally in 2025. The IEA identifies offtake uncertainty, high costs, infrastructure gaps and project cancellations/delays, and expects the 1% share to be exceeded only in 2026. LIMITATION: Global hydrogen shares cannot be presented as EU shares, and 2025 market behaviour does not causally test the 2015 CAP scenario or establish 2030 outcomes.

cases.assessment: The 2015 JRC-EU-TIMES paper treats hydrogen as a plausible decarbonisation technology where sustained carbon policy changes long-run incentives. Operational electrolysers and a developing final-investment-decision pipeline show that an industry is materialising. Deployment remains small compared with announced policy visions, and the IEA reports that low-emissions hydrogen is a tiny share of actual global output. More importantly, identified offtake and infrastructure barriers show why being technically viable in a model need not produce rapid market adoption.
cases.scope_caveat: There is still no harmonised observed EU measure of hydrogen produced, delivered and consumed in the modelled transport and industrial uses under an equivalent carbon constraint. The 2030 milestone remains ahead, and financing decisions may not result in commissioned plants or utilised assets.

interpretation.similarities: The 2015 JRC-EU-TIMES paper treats hydrogen as a plausible decarbonisation technology where sustained carbon policy changes long-run incentives. Operational electrolysers and a developing final-investment-decision pipeline show that an industry is materialising.
interpretation.differences: Deployment remains small compared with announced policy visions, and the IEA reports that low-emissions hydrogen is a tiny share of actual global output. More importantly, identified offtake and infrastructure barriers show why being technically viable in a model need not produce rapid market adoption.
interpretation.still_unestablished: There is still no harmonised observed EU measure of hydrogen produced, delivered and consumed in the modelled transport and industrial uses under an equivalent carbon constraint. The 2030 milestone remains ahead, and financing decisions may not result in commissioned plants or utilised assets.
interpretation.present_relevance: A July 2026 EU-body report provides an operational European capacity estimate and distinguishes it from 2025 investment decisions. The June 2026 IEA report adds production and end-use reality checks rather than another policy target.

research_gaps: Obtain CAP versus CPI scenario results and explicit 2030 hydrogen volumes/shares from the article’s full model tables for like-for-like testing.
Find consistent EU27 time-series data for certified low-emissions hydrogen production, actual end-use in steel/chemicals/road transport and offtake contracts through 2030.
Reconcile EU-only, geographical Europe and GW electrical input/output capacity boundaries across JRC, ACER and Clean Hydrogen JU.

proposed_corrections.existing_statement_or_source: Existing comparison of 308 MW EU operational electrolysers in 2024 with a “6 GW 2024 EU policy ambition”.
proposed_corrections.problem: An apparent gap of 308 MW versus 6 GW involves capacity definitions and political aspirations whose comparability is not self-evident; the European Court of Auditors notes unclear GW input/output definitions in the Commission’s original ambition.
proposed_corrections.proposed_correction: Label 308 MW as observed EU operational capacity and 6 GW as the separate 2024 policy ambition, noting that the audit questioned how electrolyser-capacity targets were defined. Do not use the ratio to grade the older 2015 carbon-cap model.

proposed_corrections.existing_statement_or_source: Existing JRC 2025 status figure “514–800 MW by end-2025”.
proposed_corrections.problem: It is a projected year-end range in a status report published January 2026, not a directly observed end-2025 capacity census; mixing it with commissioned MW overstates empirical comparability.
proposed_corrections.proposed_correction: Keep its explicit projection label and show the 2026 Clean Hydrogen JU observed Europe-wide >600 MW separately, noting geography and accounting differences.

cases.title: Actual and potential development of consumer demand on the organic food market in Europe
cases.source_trace: Saved original abstract, cross-checked against original publisher text. Research covered Denmark, Italy and UK and considered futures up to 2015.
cases.source_specific_proposition: A plausible scenario was continued, relatively stable expansion of organic-food demand, conditional on prices, distribution, consumer trust and public support.
cases.scenario_condition: Qualitative, conditional scenario rather than a fixed volume target.
cases.radar2_question: Did European organic-food consumer demand expand after 2011, how steadily, and do later developments support the factors originally identified?

findings.document: FiBL/AMI European organic market 2014, announced 2016
findings.evidence: Organic retail sales in Europe reached about €26.2 billion in 2014, and the three investigated markets were among the more developed markets.

findings.document: FiBL, The World of Organic Agriculture 2024 (reporting 2022)
findings.evidence: Europe-wide organic retail sales declined by about 2.2% in 2022 rather than rising every year.

findings.document: FiBL, Europe organic market 2024 data released 10 Feb 2026
findings.evidence: European organic retail sales reached €58.7 billion in 2024, above the 2014 value in nominal euros.

findings.document: Stigning i økologisk detailsalg [Increase in organic retail sales, 2024]
findings.evidence: 2024 organic grocery retail sales reached DKK 16.0 billion (+3% nominal; +2% by quantity). Organic food’s share of total food purchases fell slightly to an estimated 11.6% from 11.8% in 2023; coverage excludes farm-gate and specialist shops. LIMITATION: Food-retail aggregates do not show the household-panel reasons for choosing or dropping organic food; prices, channels and coverage are not directly the same as the 2011 sample.

findings.document: Biologico: nel 2025 gli acquisti delle famiglie volano a 4,4 miliardi di euro
findings.evidence: Italian household purchases of organic foods for home use reached €4.4 billion in 2025, +9.2% in value and +7.2% in quantities versus 2024; organic reached 4% of home food expenditure (+0.4 percentage points). These are household retail purchases rather than food-service turnover. LIMITATION: Year-on-year changes do not establish uninterrupted growth since 2011 or identify distribution, trust and price mechanisms from the older qualitative research.

findings.document: Organic Market Report 2026
findings.evidence: The 2026 UK report, launched on 4 March 2026, records £3.9 billion in organic food and drink sales in 2025 (+4.2% nominal), the fourteenth consecutive growth year by its reported UK market definition; major-retailer organic sales increased 7%. It also reports only about 3% of UK farmland is organic and domestic supply depends significantly on imports. LIMITATION: The association’s market measure is not a matched, inflation-adjusted household panel and may include UK retail channels different from Statistics Denmark or ISMEA; the launch date is corroborated by the Organic Research Centre’s 4 March 2026 launch-webinar listing.

cases.assessment: All three original markets show substantial continuing organic commerce, and the new Denmark and Italy series separate quantities from sales value. The original emphasis on retail access and prices continues to have explanatory relevance as the UK source notes supply dependence despite demand. Demand is neither uniformly stable nor identical across countries: Denmark’s organic share slipped from 2023 to 2024 even as volumes increased, whereas Italian households recorded strong 2025 volume gains. The original forecast did not specify uninterrupted annual increases, and short-term volatility is not a binary scenario refutation.
cases.scope_caveat: Comparable inflation-adjusted, category-consistent long panels for the original three markets and modern household survey data on trust, availability and organic/conventional price premia remain incomplete. None of the new country totals identifies the causal effect of public support or retail expansion on purchases.

interpretation.similarities: All three original markets show substantial continuing organic commerce, and the new Denmark and Italy series separate quantities from sales value. The original emphasis on retail access and prices continues to have explanatory relevance as the UK source notes supply dependence despite demand.
interpretation.differences: Demand is neither uniformly stable nor identical across countries: Denmark’s organic share slipped from 2023 to 2024 even as volumes increased, whereas Italian households recorded strong 2025 volume gains. The original forecast did not specify uninterrupted annual increases, and short-term volatility is not a binary scenario refutation.
interpretation.still_unestablished: Comparable inflation-adjusted, category-consistent long panels for the original three markets and modern household survey data on trust, availability and organic/conventional price premia remain incomplete. None of the new country totals identifies the causal effect of public support or retail expansion on purchases.
interpretation.present_relevance: Three dated national sources now directly cover Denmark, Italy and the UK rather than relying mainly on Europe-wide monetary aggregates. Italy provides explicit +7.2% volume growth, Denmark +2% quantity growth but falling market share, and the UK a 2025 £3.9 billion headline with supply constraints.

research_gaps: Retrieve the article’s full publisher introduction to confirm its exact 2015 expert-scenario endpoint and underlying household sample periods.
Construct harmonised 2011–2025 inflation-adjusted household organic retail volume and market-share panels for Denmark, Italy and the UK.
Test how organic/conventional price premiums, product availability, labels/trust and public conversion subsidies correlate with buyer retention across household types.

proposed_corrections.existing_statement_or_source: Existing organic demand interpretation extends the 2011 study into Europe-wide data for 2022 and 2024.
proposed_corrections.problem: The original expert exercise addressed Denmark, Italy and the UK with a short-run scenario horizon through approximately 2015, while Europe-wide later totals were not the original forecast variable.
proposed_corrections.proposed_correction: Explicitly name the original three markets and 2015 horizon and treat post-2015 observations as an extension of the question, not a precise forecast horizon or geographic validation.

proposed_corrections.existing_statement_or_source: Existing comparison “€26.2 billion in 2014” versus “€58.7 billion in 2024” for wider Europe.
proposed_corrections.problem: Both figures are nominal and aggregate different economies; reported retail turnover alone cannot prove price-adjusted demand volume growth or consistent national coverage.
proposed_corrections.proposed_correction: Keep the nominal wider-Europe comparison as context only. Use national volume changes where available and note FiBL’s data methodology, including its practice of carrying forward last available national observations for missing reporting years.

cases.title: 2022 Strategic Foresight Report: Twinning the green and digital transitions in the new geopolitical context
cases.source_trace: Original passage preserved in institutional-original-passages.json with matching source URL and date; editorial source checking still required before publication.
cases.source_specific_proposition: Strategic management and diversification of supplies of critical raw materials would be essential to the EU green and digital transitions; otherwise the EU could fall into new dependency traps.
cases.scenario_condition: A strategic warning and possible future vulnerability, not a numeric prediction.
cases.radar2_question: Did the EU recognise and act on critical raw-material dependencies after 2022, and has actual supply resilience improved?

findings.document: European Critical Raw Materials Act (in force 2024)
findings.evidence: The EU enacted policy for critical raw materials supply diversification and domestic capacity, with non-binding 2030 benchmarks for extraction, processing, recycling and single-country concentration.

findings.document: European Commission strategic-project selections under CRMA
findings.evidence: On 25 March 2025, the Commission selected EU strategic projects concerning critical raw materials supply and diversification; selection does not establish delivered supply capacity.

findings.document: European Court of Auditors, Special report 04/2026
findings.evidence: Auditors found diversification of critical raw materials supply had not yet produced tangible results, with obstacles to production and recycling and many projects unlikely to improve supply in time for 2030.

findings.document: EU trade in rare earth elements increased in 2025
findings.evidence: Eurostat customs data record 15,100 tonnes of rare-earth elements and compounds imported to the EU in 2025 (+17.1% by weight); China supplied 46.8% by weight, Russia 25.9% and Malaysia 23.1% (dataset ds-045409). This is a narrow traded-product classification, not all critical raw materials or an accounting of finished rare-earth magnets. LIMITATION: Partner shares of import tonnage cannot be assumed to equal EU total consumption, concentration by material or the CRMA single-country benchmark; they do not prove causal effects of any legislation.

findings.document: Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026: executive summary
findings.evidence: IEA reports Chinese controls imposed on seven heavy rare-earth elements in April 2025 caused some downstream automakers to reduce production rates or temporarily halt operations. It also documents approximately fivefold European-versus-China prices for gallium and some heavy rare earths in 2026, while noting a modest decline in rare-earth refining concentration due to output in Malaysia and the US. LIMITATION: The IEA is describing global supply networks and price markets, not isolating EU-only throughput or the effects of the foresight publication; controls and industrial responses do not establish attribution to EU policy.

cases.assessment: The 2022 report anticipated a structural tension between the EU’s green/digital aims and geographically concentrated inputs. Later EU rules, strategy designations, import records and independent IEA monitoring show that the dependency issue remains a live strategic priority. A significant new development is the realised production disruption following 2025 Chinese heavy rare-earth export controls, rather than merely a theoretical dependence ratio. The IEA nevertheless observes some modest rare-earth refining diversification, so the picture is not one-way worsening in every mineral.
cases.scope_caveat: The EU’s material-by-material supply security, magnet imports, downstream component dependence, recycling yields and new mine/refinery actual outputs are not established by aggregate REE customs tonnage. Whether CRMA programmes durably lower vulnerability by 2030, and what role the 2022 foresight document had in policymaking, remain separate open questions.
cases.original_excerpt: Strategically managing supply of critical materials and commodities, by adopting a long-term systemic approach to avoid a new dependency trap.

passage_review.note: Exact wording of area for action 3 on the original 2022 Commission strategic foresight report webpage.

interpretation.similarities: The 2022 report anticipated a structural tension between the EU’s green/digital aims and geographically concentrated inputs. Later EU rules, strategy designations, import records and independent IEA monitoring show that the dependency issue remains a live strategic priority.
interpretation.differences: A significant new development is the realised production disruption following 2025 Chinese heavy rare-earth export controls, rather than merely a theoretical dependence ratio. The IEA nevertheless observes some modest rare-earth refining diversification, so the picture is not one-way worsening in every mineral.
interpretation.still_unestablished: The EU’s material-by-material supply security, magnet imports, downstream component dependence, recycling yields and new mine/refinery actual outputs are not established by aggregate REE customs tonnage. Whether CRMA programmes durably lower vulnerability by 2030, and what role the 2022 foresight document had in policymaking, remain separate open questions.
interpretation.present_relevance: Eurostat contributes a dated 2025 EU import partner distribution, while the IEA contributes observed 2025 disruptions and a 2026 downstream price premium. These are outcome and vulnerability measures beyond the case’s existing legal acts, project selections and 2026 audit.

research_gaps: Obtain EU end-to-end material balances for each strategic raw material, including magnets, processed compounds and indirect imports embedded in finished goods.
Track CRMA designated projects from approval through permitting, financing, commissioning and verified annual output.
Find a documented legislative or Commission preparatory citation before stating the 2022 foresight report directly influenced the CRMA.

proposed_corrections.existing_statement_or_source: Existing description of CRMA 2030 “single-country concentration” benchmarks and selected strategic projects.
proposed_corrections.problem: The 2025 Eurostat rare-earth import shares are a by-weight classification of selected metals and compounds; neither they nor counts of approved projects directly quantify attainment of the CRMA’s strategic-raw-material sourcing/diversification benchmark.
proposed_corrections.proposed_correction: When using the new 46.8% China import share, add “selected REE traded categories, by gross weight” and retain the separate interpretation of CRMA project designations as policy steps, not measured diversification outcomes.

cases.title: Suitability of European climate for the Asian tiger mosquito Aedes albopictus: recent trends and future scenarios
cases.source_trace: Original 2012 Royal Society paper abstract checked against PubMed PMID 22535696; source passage preserved in the accepted Radar 1 manifest.
cases.source_specific_proposition: The 2012 climate-suitability scenarios suggested growing risk of Aedes albopictus establishment in northern and north-western Europe, while parts of southern Europe might become less climatically suitable under hotter, drier conditions.
cases.scenario_condition: Conditional projections of climatic suitability, not a forecast of the exact number of established mosquito populations or direct proof of climate-driven spread.
cases.radar2_question: Did Aedes albopictus become established farther north and west in Europe after 2012, and can changes in its distribution be linked specifically to the projected climatic mechanisms?

findings.document: ECDC/EFSA: Aedes albopictus known distribution, June 2025 (published 1 July 2025)
findings.evidence: ECDC reported established Asian tiger mosquito populations in 369 EU/EEA administrative regions across 16 countries, including Belgium, Germany and Austria; it noted newly established populations in Cyprus and Slovakia since the July 2024 update.

findings.document: ECDC/EFSA: Aedes albopictus current known distribution, April 2026 (published 3 June 2026)
findings.evidence: The updated ECDC surveillance map listed established populations in 384 EU/EEA administrative units in 16 countries, fourteen additional units compared with June 2025; the geographic spread remains documented in northern and western EU countries as well as in southern Europe.

findings.document: Farooq et al., The Lancet Planetary Health: Impact of climate and Aedes albopictus establishment on dengue and chikungunya outbreaks in Europe (May 2025)
findings.evidence: A peer-reviewed EU regional analysis of 1990–2024 entomological and outbreak data found shorter intervals between mosquito establishment and first local arbovirus outbreak. Warm-summer conditions were associated with increased outbreak hazard, but this is not proof that temperature alone caused the species to spread north.

findings.document: Non-native mosquito species profiles: Aedes albopictus
findings.evidence: UKHSA states the Asian tiger mosquito has not established a self-sustaining population in the UK despite eggs having been detected in southeast England through invasive-mosquito surveillance since 2016. LIMITATION: UK non-establishment cannot be explained by temperature alone; surveillance effort, introduction frequency, local habitat and vector control may all matter.

findings.document: Seasonal surveillance of chikungunya virus disease – 2026 (weekly), 11 September update
findings.evidence: The 11 September 2026 ECDC snapshot, covering notifications as of 9 September, identifies 57 locally acquired chikungunya cases in France across 11 clusters and one case in Italy (Rome). LIMITATION: Local human cases are not a direct measure of Aedes albopictus climatic suitability or unambiguous evidence that climate change drove a given outbreak; human travel, virus importation, local surveillance and vector control contribute.

cases.assessment: Observed establishment across central and north-western continental Europe agrees broadly with the direction of the original climate-suitability warning. New ECDC disease surveillance shows actual local transmission in France and Italy, which makes vector readiness a continuing public-health concern. The UK is a useful exception: repeated egg introductions have not yet translated into recognised population establishment. Disease episodes are also a different phenomenon from the paper’s climatic thresholds, while the projected slight decline in southern suitability is not directly refuted by continued southern establishment.
cases.scope_caveat: Comparable climate-adjusted longitudinal suitability estimates, surveillance-normalised establishment histories and estimates of the impact of transport and interventions are not available from the regional counts alone. The source-level 369-to-384 versus “14 additions” discrepancy also needs a documented crosswalk.

interpretation.similarities: Observed establishment across central and north-western continental Europe agrees broadly with the direction of the original climate-suitability warning. New ECDC disease surveillance shows actual local transmission in France and Italy, which makes vector readiness a continuing public-health concern.
interpretation.differences: The UK is a useful exception: repeated egg introductions have not yet translated into recognised population establishment. Disease episodes are also a different phenomenon from the paper’s climatic thresholds, while the projected slight decline in southern suitability is not directly refuted by continued southern establishment.
interpretation.still_unestablished: Comparable climate-adjusted longitudinal suitability estimates, surveillance-normalised establishment histories and estimates of the impact of transport and interventions are not available from the regional counts alone. The source-level 369-to-384 versus “14 additions” discrepancy also needs a documented crosswalk.
interpretation.present_relevance: New UKHSA evidence explicitly distinguishes introductions from established populations, and September 2026 ECDC surveillance independently tracks indigenous chikungunya transmission. These go beyond the existing EU/EEA establishment maps and the retrospective association study.

research_gaps: Map the 2012 model grids against contemporary seasonal climate observations and site-level confirmed overwintering, holding surveillance intensity constant.
Reconcile ECDC’s 2025 369 and 2026 384 totals with its narrative of 14 added units and any revised country/regional coding.
Investigate southern Europe suitability trends using temperature, summer precipitation, irrigation and larval habitat observations rather than equating establishment with suitability.

proposed_corrections.existing_statement_or_source: Existing ECDC 2026 description: “384 EU/EEA administrative units ... fourteen additional units compared with June 2025” after listing 369 in 2025.
proposed_corrections.problem: Arithmetic gives a net difference of 15 units (384 minus 369), whereas the 2026 ECDC narrative explicitly reports an expansion of 14 named units across five countries; the published description does not reconcile the two figures.
proposed_corrections.proposed_correction: Quote the 384 total and ECDC’s independently stated “14 expansion units” separately rather than equating 14 to the total net change; flag the +15-versus-14 reconciliation for dataset-level checking (e.g., revised geography or previously counted units).

cases.title: Assessing the impact of the 2011 EU Transport White Paper - a rail freight demand forecast up to 2050 for the EU27
cases.source_trace: Full original article checked on Springer Nature; published online 19 June 2015 (Radar 1 indexed date 18 June 2015). The optimistic scenario is conditional on EU White Paper modal-shift ambitions.
cases.source_specific_proposition: The 2015 TRANS-TOOLS analysis compared a Reference, a White Paper Low and a White Paper High scenario. Under full achievement of ambitious EU freight modal-shift objectives, the High scenario yielded rail-freight demand nearly twice the Reference scenario by 2050.
cases.scenario_condition: The High case assumes policy implementation, infrastructure capacity and a shift of long-distance freight over 300 km from road toward rail and inland waterways. It is not an unconditional prediction of 2024 modal shares.
cases.radar2_question: Does observed EU rail freight development since 2015 indicate movement toward the ambitious road-to-rail modal shift, and which assumptions of the original High scenario remain unmet?

findings.document: European Environment Agency, Sustainability of Europe’s mobility systems 2025: freight transport activity
findings.evidence: EEA reported rail freight activity of about 396 billion tonne-kilometres in 2023, below its approximately 432 billion tonne-kilometre 2018 peak; rail represented 11.5% of all freight tonne-kilometres under the EEA indicator definition.

findings.document: German Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), EU rail freight modal split, updated 17 March 2026
findings.evidence: Drawing on Eurostat inland-transport data, Destatis reported rail accounted for approximately 17% of EU inland freight tonne-kilometres in 2024, while road accounted for roughly 78%, up from about 74% in 2014. The hoped-for modal shift was not visible in this broad indicator.

findings.document: Rail freight transport dropped by 1.8% in 2025
findings.evidence: Eurostat’s main-railway-undertakings series (rail_go_typepas) reports 368.2 billion EU tonne-kilometres in 2025, down 1.8% from 375.1 billion in 2024; this marks a fourth consecutive yearly fall in the series. Reporting thresholds exclude smaller railway undertakings. LIMITATION: EU27 activity from main operators cannot be compared mechanically with the EEA all-freight estimate or a model-generated 2050 EU27 difference between counterfactual scenarios.

findings.document: EU road freight transport up by 0.9% in 2025
findings.evidence: Road freight work performed by EU-registered vehicles reached 1,886 billion tonne-kilometres in 2025, +0.9% from 2024 (dataset road_go_ta_tott). Its road-registration data basis differs from rail national-operator data and route-specific road-to-rail modal-shift measures. LIMITATION: National registration, international/cabotage activity, freight-distance classes and railway reporting thresholds differ; this is not a direct measurement of White Paper freight over 300 km.

findings.document: Intermodal freight transport: EU still far from getting freight off the road, Special Report 08/2023
findings.evidence: ECA examined EU intermodal transport support including €1.1 billion committed in 2014–2020 and 16 sampled projects across seven countries. It judged modal-shift targets unrealistic/insufficiently monitored, identified terminal, legal and interoperability barriers, and found that funded infrastructure projects were primarily monitored for outputs, not measured tonnes shifted from road (executive summary III–VI; paragraphs 83–89). LIMITATION: The 2023 audit covers support and sampled intermodal projects, not all EU rail traffic and not the TRANS-TOOLS model itself; it cannot directly estimate the High-versus-Reference rail-demand outcome.

cases.assessment: The original model emphasised the scale of institutional and infrastructure change required for major rail growth, not an inevitable doubling. Both recent activity data and an institutional audit confirm that those prerequisites remain pivotal. Eurostat records 2025 road-freight activity rising while main-operator rail-freight work fell for the fourth year. ECA’s finding that targets were not robustly monitored, and that terminals and interoperability hamper competition, illustrates why policy aspirations do not automatically generate modal shift.
cases.scope_caveat: The distance-specific >300 km road-freight base, measured diversion to rail or waterways, freight terminal productivity and a harmonised EU27 Reference path remain missing. The 2030 and 2050 policy horizons also remain open; no 2025 all-freight statistic is a direct test of the model’s 2050 High scenario.

interpretation.similarities: The original model emphasised the scale of institutional and infrastructure change required for major rail growth, not an inevitable doubling. Both recent activity data and an institutional audit confirm that those prerequisites remain pivotal.
interpretation.differences: Eurostat records 2025 road-freight activity rising while main-operator rail-freight work fell for the fourth year. ECA’s finding that targets were not robustly monitored, and that terminals and interoperability hamper competition, illustrates why policy aspirations do not automatically generate modal shift.
interpretation.still_unestablished: The distance-specific >300 km road-freight base, measured diversion to rail or waterways, freight terminal productivity and a harmonised EU27 Reference path remain missing. The 2030 and 2050 policy horizons also remain open; no 2025 all-freight statistic is a direct test of the model’s 2050 High scenario.
interpretation.present_relevance: Two Eurostat 2026 releases bring activity measurement through 2025, while the ECA’s intermodal audit provides concrete reasons for slow implementation. An online publisher date correction and metric-denominator clarification improve auditability of the older comparison.

research_gaps: Find a measured EU-wide >300 km road-freight modal shift time series compatible with the 2011 White Paper target.
Recreate model Reference and High assumptions using up-to-date input costs, capacity, terminals and infrastructure delays, without treating the replay as the 2015 prediction.
Reconcile rail_go_typepas, EEA cross-modal estimates and national registration-based road tonne-km accounting before creating a modal split.

proposed_corrections.existing_statement_or_source: Existing comparison cites EEA 2023 rail share 11.5% and Destatis/Eurostat inland rail share about 17% in 2024.
proposed_corrections.problem: EEA 11.5% includes broader modes such as coastal maritime freight, while Destatis 17% is a rail share among inland road/rail/waterway tonne-km; these are not competing measurements of the same denominator.
proposed_corrections.proposed_correction: Display the two percentages with their distinct mode coverage and years, and assess change only within a harmonised single series; neither evaluates the >300 km modal-shift promise.

proposed_corrections.existing_statement_or_source: Original lead dated 18 June 2015 in the curated entry.
proposed_corrections.problem: The publisher’s article header says “Published: 19 June 2015”, one day after the recorded historical date.
proposed_corrections.proposed_correction: Use 19 June 2015 as verified online publication date, preserving 18 June only if a distinct traceable indexing/acceptance event is found.

cases.title: Ocean energy development in Europe: Current status and future perspectives
cases.source_trace: Original open-access publisher record checked. The 2015 article describes a sectoral ambition of 100 GW wave-and-tidal capacity by 2050; this is an aspiration reported by the authors, not an unconditional model result.
cases.source_specific_proposition: The 2015 assessment envisaged wave and tidal energy as a potentially substantial contributor to Europe’s future low-carbon electricity system and described a sectoral aim of 100 GW by 2050, conditional on overcoming technology, financing, grid and regulatory barriers.
cases.scenario_condition: A long-term ambition contingent on technology readiness, finance and market development. The objective’s definition and geographical scope need checking before numerical target comparisons.
cases.radar2_question: Did wave and tidal energy move toward large-scale commercial deployment in the EU after 2015, and which originally recognised deployment barriers persist?

findings.document: European Commission DG MARE, EU Blue Economy Report 2025: marine renewable energy
findings.evidence: At the end of 2024, the EU had about 2.82 MW of operational emerging ocean-energy capacity excluding traditional tidal-range projects, including 1.63 MW tidal energy and 1.12 MW wave energy. These technologies remained at demonstration or emerging deployment scale.

findings.document: European Commission Joint Research Centre, Ocean Energy in the European Union — 2025 Status Report (10 December 2025)
findings.evidence: The JRC reviewed the tidal and wave sector’s technical development, EU-funded projects, market progress and bottlenecks through the end of 2024. It identified risks and obstacles to the long-term technology targets, rather than documenting commercial deployment on the original hoped-for scale.

findings.document: Ocean Energy Europe, Ocean energy is moving closer to commercialisation (17 April 2025)
findings.evidence: The European industry association reported five wave and tidal ocean-energy developers deploying new devices in 2024 and a publicly supported 165 MW ocean-energy pipeline planned for deployment over the following five years. These European plans are not operational EU electricity-generating capacity and must not be counted as deployment achieved.

findings.document: Marine Renewable Energy: Ocean Energy, Blue Economy Observatory (2026 update)
findings.evidence: The Commission’s ocean-energy section reports 2.2 MW operational EU non-tidal-range ocean capacity at end-2025 *excluding pilot projects*: 1.5 MW tidal stream, 0.65 MW wave and 0.02 MW salinity gradient. It separately reports 2024 EU ocean-electricity production of 461 GWh, 449 GWh from La Rance tidal barrage and only 12 GWh from other technologies (Ocean Energy subsection, Figure 5; update 21 May 2026). LIMITATION: Its end-2025 “excluding pilot projects” boundary may differ from the 2024 existing-record 2.82 MW category, and La Rance tidal-range production is not comparable to emerging tidal-stream/wave output. Annual GWh and installed/operational MW cannot be converted without technology-specific utilisation factors.

findings.document: Europe’s ocean energy pipeline reaches 200 devices and 200 MW as public funding leverages private investment
findings.evidence: The association reports sixteen publicly supported European wave/tidal farm projects totalling 196 MW *expected* by 2030: eleven tidal farms with 172 MW and 140 devices and five wave farms with 24 MW and 66 devices. It separately reports aspirational national commitments of another 650 MW; none of these MW is verified as operational. LIMITATION: The European industry pipeline includes the UK and has scope/date differences from the earlier 165 MW set. It is developer/association reporting of intentions and subsidies, not evidence of generation, completed capacity, commercially viable tariffs or EU-only deployment.

cases.assessment: The original 2015 assessment connected ocean-energy potential to technology maturity, market support, financing and grid conditions. EU monitoring and industry reporting continue to identify noncommercial costs and public revenue support as central to progress. The dominant observed fact remains a tiny operational wave/tidal fleet in the EU, now complemented by just 12 GWh of 2024 non-tidal-range generation; the old La Rance barrage contributes most measured EU ocean electricity. Meanwhile a more substantial 196 MW European pre-commercial pipeline is emerging, but financial commitment and device plans do not equal electricity delivered.
cases.scope_caveat: Individual device operating hours, capacity factors, decommissioning/replacement cycles, delivered grid output and realised levelised costs are needed to establish actual commercial progress. Comparability across “excluding pilots”, tidal-range inclusion, EU versus Europe and the sector’s 2050 100 GW ambition is unresolved without an explicit taxonomy.

findings.document: Share of energy from renewable sources in transport (nrg_ind_ren, REN_TRA): EU27_2020
findings.evidence: Renewable energy share in transport (RES-T): 1.8% (2005), 5.5% (2010), 10.3% (2020), 9.6% (2022), 11.0% (2023), 11.2% (2024). Extracted via the Eurostat API on 2026-10-26. findings.document: Greenhouse gas emissions from transport in Europe (EEA indicator)
findings.evidence: EEA states that EU transport emissions "have only declined slightly since 2005" and that preliminary 2024 emissions were 0.7% above 2023; road transport emitted 73% of EU transport GHG (incl. international bunkers) in 2023. Member State projections: with existing measures transport emissions would reach 1990 levels by 2030; with additional measures 13% below 1990 (Figure 1 and Figure 2 text). LIMITATION: Compares one projection with another; the page mixes 'domestic' wording with a methodology that sums 1.A.3 plus international aviation and maritime, so the scope of the 2030 projection is ambiguous. cases.assessment: Observed EU transport emissions did not follow the reference path (+17%); by 2024 domestic transport emissions were about 5% below 2005, the direction of the integrated scenario. Renewable shares in transport reached about 10% around 2020, close to the integrated run's preliminary 2020 biofuel figure. Progress was slower than the integrated path: emissions were only 1.8% below 2005 in 2019, and then COVID-19 (2020) and the 2022 energy shock caused swings that neither scenario represented. International aviation emissions grew about 35% (2005-2024), a part of transport outside the domestic total.

findings.evidence: World newsprint production fell from 33.1 Mt (2010) to 10.6 Mt (2024, estimate; -68%); graphic papers from 143.3 Mt to 85.1 Mt (-41%). LIMITATION: The decline was already under way in 2011, so this continues a trend more than it confirms a forecast. findings.document: FAOSTAT Forestry Production and Trade: Sweden, production of paper grades, sawnwood and wood pellets
findings.evidence: Sweden: graphic papers 5.51 Mt (2010) -> 1.81 Mt (2024, estimate; -67%); newsprint 2.26 Mt -> 0.22 Mt (-90%); total paper and paperboard 11.41 Mt -> 8.07 Mt (-29%); other paper and paperboard 5.90 Mt -> 6.26 Mt (+6%). findings.document: TMF i siffror - Statistik om den svenska trä- och möbelindustrin, nr 1, April 2026
findings.evidence: p. 3: according to SCB, 1,393 ordinary apartments with wooden frames were started in 2024 (-6.8% vs 2023), and the wood-frame share of all started apartments in multi-dwelling buildings rose to 17% in 2024; 95.4% of wood-frame apartments were fully or partly prefabricated ('helt eller delvis förtillverkade'). TMF's industrial wood-frame producers delivered 2,339 apartments in 2025 (-1.1% vs 2024). LIMITATION: Industry-association digest relaying SCB data (not independently checked against SCB tables). Covers started ordinary apartments only, excluding student and special housing, and is a single year of share data. Energy efficiency and value added for sawmills are not measured, and no causal link to the paper.

cases.assessment: The paper's most robust expectation, steep ICT-driven decline in newsprint and printing paper, is clearly observed both globally (-41% graphic papers 2010-2024) and in Sweden (-67%). Industrially prefabricated timber frames dominate Swedish wood multi-dwelling construction and reached a 17% share of started apartments in 2024. Swedish sawnwood volumes have been flat rather than growing, and pellet output has not expanded, so the bioenergy-driven 'demand pressure on Swedish wood' of scenarios II-IV is not evident in production volumes. Packaging-paper growth, which the paper did not emphasise, cushioned the pulp and paper sector.

Value-added and profitability outcomes for Swedish sawmills, and forest-owner wood prices, were not examined.

findings.document: Data en feiten 2014 - Het jaar 2013 in cijfers
findings.evidence: Section 1.2 'Gebruik van geneesmiddelen' (PDF p. 14) and summary: medicine use from community pharmacies, measured in DDD, grew 1.1% in 2013, whereas population growth and ageing alone implied +1.9%; annual growth over the preceding decade had been about 4-8% (summary) or 4-5% (Section 1.2). People aged 65+ (17.4% of the population on 1 Jan 2014) received more than three times the average volume. SFK offers healthier new 65+ cohorts and the rise in the insurance deductible (EUR 155 -> 350, 2009-2013) as possible explanations. LIMITATION: Single-year comparison. Measured in DDD of reimbursed medicines, not tonnes of active substance; the +1.9% expectation is SFK's own calculation, not the paper's. SFK's explanations are offered as possibilities, not tested.

findings.document: Data en feiten 2025 - Het jaar 2024 in cijfers
findings.evidence: Section 1.2, p. 21 and Figure 1.2: community pharmacies dispensed almost 8.9 billion DDD of reimbursed medicines in 2024 (+2.7% vs 2023, against estimated population growth of ~0.7%), i.e. 532 DDD per head (+2.0%). People aged 75+ used 1,574 DDD per head versus the 532 average. The largest per-head increase (+2.7%) was among 21-40-year-olds, driven by ADHD medicines (methylphenidate +10%, lisdexamfetamine +38%) and sertraline (+10%). LIMITATION: DDD volume, not mass of active substance (the paper's unit), and reimbursed community-pharmacy medicines only. A single year, so it cannot be compared with the paper's 2020 tonnage projection without conversion.

findings.document: Directive (EU) 2024/3019 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 November 2024 concerning urban wastewater treatment (recast)
findings.evidence: Entered into force 1 Jan 2025 (transposition by 31 Jul 2027). It requires quaternary treatment (micropollutant removal) at plants of 150,000 p.e. and above: 20% of such plants by 31 Dec 2033, 60% by 31 Dec 2039 and all by 31 Dec 2045. Producers of medicinal products for human use and cosmetics must cover at least 80% of the additional treatment costs (extended producer responsibility). EurEau reported on 2026-02-20 that the EU General Court dismissed industry challenges to the EPR provisions as inadmissible. LIMITATION: No documented influence of this paper on the Directive. It is EU-wide, not Dutch-specific, implementation lies in the future, and cost-sharing remains politically contested.

findings.document: Disparity in elevational shifts of European trees in response to recent climate warming
findings.evidence: Juvenile vs adult altitudinal distributions of seven major European tree species on transects from southern Spain (37°N) to northern Sweden (67°N), where mean temperature over the last decade was 0.86 °C above the previous 30-year period. Only Abies alba showed juveniles peaking higher than adults. Fagus sylvatica, Picea abies and Pinus sylvestris showed the opposite pattern, and no change was detected for Quercus ilex, Acer pseudoplatanus and Q. petraea. The authors state that the findings are 'in contrast with theoretical predictions'. LIMITATION: Elevational juvenile-adult comparison, not latitudinal range-front migration. Limited transects and species, whose overlap with Meier et al.'s 14 species was not verified. Abstract-level check.

findings.document: Species better track climate warming in the oceans than on land
findings.evidence: BioShifts geodatabase of 30,534 range shifts (over 12,000 species): marine species shift poleward about six times faster than terrestrial ones, and terrestrial species lag behind shifting isotherms more than marine species. 'On land, human activities impede the capacity of terrestrial species to track isotherm shifts in latitude'; elevational shifts follow isotherms but more slowly than expected. The data are biased toward developed Northern Hemisphere regions. LIMITATION: Global, multi-taxa synthesis; no tree- or Europe-specific estimate was checked. Heterogeneous underlying studies, and it does not test the TreeMig-derived rates.

findings.document: Excess forest mortality is consistently linked to drought across Europe
findings.evidence: Satellite canopy-mortality maps for 1987-2016 show excess forest mortality significantly related to drought across continental Europe, with threshold behaviour: steep increases when the March-July climatic water balance falls below -1.6 SD. Drought caused about 500,000 ha of excess mortality, and the authors suggest that more drought could trigger widespread tree mortality. LIMITATION: Mortality is not resolved by species in this analysis and does not test Meier et al.'s projections. The study period ends in 2016, before the 2018-2020 central European drought years.

cases.assessment: Observational syntheses since 2011 support the core premise that terrestrial species, especially under human land-use constraints, lag behind shifting climate. European field data show several mid- to late-successional trees not shifting upslope, consistent in direction with the projected very slow migration. Some species show juveniles at lower, not higher, elevations than adults, implying demographic or ontogenetic controls not represented in the migration model. Drought-driven mortality emerged as a major, abrupt driver of forest change, outside the model's colonisation-focused framing.
cases.scope_caveat: The projection horizon (21st century) is far off, and no study was found that directly evaluates the predicted migration rates for the same 14 species. Distinguishing slow migration from non-climatic causes in observed distributions remains methodologically hard.

findings.document: Population on 1 January (demo_pjan) and population structure indicators (demo_pjanind): Bulgaria
findings.evidence: Bulgaria's population was 7,369,431 (2011), 6,532,117 (2021) and 6,437,360 (2025), -12.6% over 2011-2025. The 65+ share rose from 18.5% to 23.0% to 24.0%, the old-age dependency ratio from 27.0 to 36.7 to 38.7, and the median age from 42.5 (2011) to 47.3 (2025). Extracted via the Eurostat API on 2026-10-26. LIMITATION: Demographic outcomes do not validate the productivity link. The series may be affected by census-based revisions (2021 census), and the paper's life-expectancy variants were not compared with outturns.

findings.document: Labour productivity and unit labour costs (nama_10_lp_ulc): real labour productivity, Bulgaria and EU27_2020
findings.evidence: Real labour productivity per person (index 2015=100): Bulgaria 93.5 (2011), 111.4 (2019), 123.7 (2024), i.e. +32% over 2011-2024; EU27 98.0 to 104.7 (+7%). Per hour worked: Bulgaria 93.5 to 125.1 (+34%); EU27 96.4 to 106.0 (+10%). Extracted via the Eurostat API on 2026-10-26. LIMITATION: Per-person productivity can rise through composition effects (exit or emigration of lower-productivity workers, sectoral shifts). With no counterfactual this neither tests nor contradicts the ILO-model sensitivity result.

findings.document: Economic Aspects of Demographic Changes in the European Union and in Bulgaria
findings.evidence: pp. 45-46 restate ILO-model results to 2050 under three life-expectancy variants, citing Rangelova & Sariiski (2013), 'Ageing in Bulgaria', pp. 124-139. Differences in GDP per employed person across variants are '(albeit very small)', and faster life-expectancy improvement goes with lower productivity. The authors call the negative ageing effect '(though unconvincing)' yet 'confirmed', and urge caution because the model is 'a simple extrapolation of current trends'. LIMITATION: Author self-assessment, not independent. It cites a 2013 publication; whether that is identical to or an update of the 2011 SEER analysis was not verified.

cases.assessment: Bulgaria's demographic decline and ageing proceeded strongly (population -12.6% and 65+ share 18.5% to 24.0%, 2011-2025). Later work, including the same author (2019) and a Bulgarian National Bank model study (DP/124/2025, Ivanov, Cvetkova & Vassilev), still treats shrinking labour input as a lasting drag on potential growth. Observed real labour productivity rose about 32% (2011-2024), more than four times the EU average, despite ageing. The lead author later described the modelled negative ageing effect on productivity as small and 'unconvincing'.
cases.scope_caveat: No counterfactual analysis isolating the effect of workforce ageing on Bulgarian productivity since 2011 was found. The 2050 horizon has not arrived, and the ILO model's projected productivity path could not be compared numerically because the full text was not accessible.
